title: Biobehavioral Investigations on Cooking: Measuring Biobehavioral and Neural Measurements in Cooking
official: Biobehavioral Investigations on Cooking: A Pilot Study to Measure Biobehavioral and Neural Measurements in Cooking
summary:
Background:

Cooking at home is a good way for a person to eat a healthy diet. Some people enjoy cooking, whereas others find it stressful. Researchers want to know more about how brain activity affects emotional and physical responses when people cook.

Objective:

To learn how the brain works when people cook.

Eligibility:

People aged 25 to 55 years who are right handed. Both professional cooks and people who cook only at home are needed.

Design:

Participants will have 3 or 4 clinic visits.

Day 1: They will give samples of blood, saliva, and a tongue brushing. They will report everything they ate over the past 24 hours. They will have a functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) scan: They will watch videos of cooking and other activities during the scan.

Day 2: They will cook a dish they know well 4 times. During each cooking event, 2 of these conditions will occur:

Either (1) they will wear a cap with sensors to measure electrical activity in the brain (EEG) or (2) they will wear different devices to monitor heart rate, sweat glands, eye movements, and other measures of stress. Also, either (1) they will cook their dish in their usual way or (2) they will follow instructions from the study team.

Day 3: They will cook their dish 2 times, while wearing the EEG and the other monitoring devices at the same time. They will cook once their own way, and once following instructions.

Day 4 is optional. Participants will drink a breakfast shake, then have some physical and memory tests. Then they will select portion sizes of food they would like to eat.
criteria:
* INCLUSION CRITERIA:

To be eligible to participate in this study, an individual must meet all the following criteria:

1. Aged 25-55 years.
2. Right-handed.
3. English-language ability in speaking and reading
4. Stated willingness to comply with all study procedures including willingness to cook and taste foods during the study.
5. Stated familiarity with potential foods and recipes used in the cooking tasks.
6. For professional cooks: completion of culinary arts training and currently working within a professional kitchen environment part time or full time for at least two years.
7. For non-cooks: cooking on average no more than two times a week for the last two years where cooking is defined as transformation or modification of food ingredients, no prior professional culinary education or training.
8. Live within a U.S. geographic location.

EXCLUSION CRITERIA:

An individual who meets any of the following criteria will be excluded from participation in this study:

1. Non-English speaking
2. Diagnosis of or treatment for (current or within the prior 12 months) anxiety, major depressive disorder or related mental health disorders.
3. Diagnosis (current or within the prior 12 months) of diabetes or heart disease conditions.
4. Diagnosis (current or ever history of) cerebrovascular accident, traumatic brain injury, or sleep apnea, seizure disorders, schizophrenic disorders, or bipolar disorders
5. Current or within the past 12 months smokers of cigarettes, cigars, vaping agents, or e-cigarettes.
6. Medication or supplement use within the prior 6 weeks for mood disorders, such as selective serotonin inhibitors, tricyclic antidepressants, benzodiazepines, and opioids.
7. Medication or supplement use within the prior 6 weeks for seizure disorders, such as anticonvulsant drugs, also known as antiepileptic drugs (AEDs).
8. Individuals taking (within the prior 6 weeks) glucocorticoid medications (oral, nasal or ophthalmic), medications that increase salivary cortisol levels (i.e. phosphodiesterase inhibitors), antibiotics or supplements that interfere with cortisol measurement, such as

   phosphatidylcholine supplements.
9. Diagnosis of mageirocophobia (cooking phobia) or a related condition of obsessive-compulsive disorder.
10. Self-reported allergies to any of the food ingredients in the selected food task or an individual with any nut (including tree nut), dairy, soy, wheat, eggs allergy.
11. Diagnosis of lactose intolerance
12. Women who are pregnant; women who are breastfeeding.
13. Individuals with xerostomia, dysgeusia, anosmia, or parosmia or associated health conditions (e.g. Sjogren's syndrome).
14. Inability to ambulate and stand for consecutive time period of at least 20 minutes in order to complete and move within the kitchen unaided and complete experimental tasks without a break.
15. Individuals with a body mass index (BMI) over 30 kg/m\^2 due to obesity-related alterations in the brain s dopamine system, which may affect neural responses to food and confound measurement of typical reward processing.
16. Individuals who report having more than 7 drinks/week for women and 14 drinks/week for men on average, and/or report regular use of cannabis.
17. Individuals who are not able to have an MRI due to claustrophobia or presence of metal or devices located within the body of the individual that prohibit MRI from being conducted.
